tagline: A road along Ouachita crests connects forest overlooks with railroad resort history.
intro: Talimena Scenic Drive follows the crests of Winding Stair and Rich Mountain between Talihina, Oklahoma, and Mena, Arkansas. The 54-mile road curves through the Ouachita National Forest on two lanes, with 22 vista pull-outs. Grades reach at least 13 percent, and many of the forests along the ridges are stunted old growth that was never logged. A National Scenic Byway since 2005, it offers views of the Ouachitas’ east-west ranges, highlighted by the Forest Service, and fall foliage noted by Arkansas’s transportation department. The Federal Highway Administration suggests one to two driving hours, or five hours with stops.

The present road opened in 1969, forming part of what would become Oklahoma State Highway 1. Lucy Baines Johnson-Nugent, Lyndon B. Johnson’s daughter, dedicated it in June 1970. Recognition followed in stages: National Forest Scenic Byway in 1989, then Arkansas state designation in 1998 and Oklahoma state designation in 2002.

Begin near Talimena State Park, northeast of Talihina, and follow Oklahoma Highway 1 east along the ridges. Castle Rock and Sugarloaf are among the scenic turnouts on the Oklahoma stretch. Arkansas’s portion runs 18 miles between the state line and Highway 71 in Mena. Across the state line, Highway 88 continues along Rich Mountain past Queen Wilhelmina State Park before descending into Mena.

moments.title: Winding Stair Mountains
moments.text: Winding Stair is a ridge within the Ouachita Mountains, with peaks reaching about 2,400 feet. During territorial times, these mountains formed the boundary between Sugar Loaf and Wade counties in the Choctaw Nation. The range now lies almost entirely within the Ouachita National Forest. Native trees include shortleaf pine, white oak and flowering dogwood. The scenic drive crosses the ridge, while Highway 1 bisects the Winding Stair Mountain National Recreation Area, created in 1988. The recreation area contains campgrounds and a lake, as well as a 45-mile section of the Ouachita National Recreation Trail.

moments.title: Queen Wilhelmina State Park
moments.text: The lodge on Rich Mountain is the third built here. The Kansas City, Pittsburg and Gulf Railroad opened the original in June 1898 to accommodate passengers. With many Dutch investors, the railroad named it for Queen Wilhelmina, whose coronation was scheduled for September. The inn closed permanently in 1910. Arkansas created the state park in 1957, after interest in tourism increased following World War II. A replacement opened in 1963, incorporating some original stonework, but a kitchen fire destroyed it ten years later. The third lodge opened in 1975 and reopened after refurbishment in 2015, continuing the site’s lodging role.

moments.title: Mena
moments.text: Mena’s railroad both brought jobs and took them away. Arthur Edward Stilwell founded the town while building the Kansas City, Pittsburg and Gulf Railroad, and train service began in 1896. He named it for Folmina Margaretha Janssen-De Goeijen, his financier’s wife, known to her husband as Mena. Timber, farming and mineral extraction were the area’s main industries as the railroad town developed. The town grew to 3,423 people by 1900. Ten years later, moving the railroad shops to Heavener cost Mena eight hundred jobs. Janssen Park in the town center also carries the name of the woman honored by Mena’s name.
